title: In-Order Cursor Over a Search Tree
statement:
Build a cursor that walks a binary search tree in ascending order, one value at a time, like a lazy iterator.

  • TreeCursor(root) takes the root of a binary search tree with distinct values. The cursor starts before the smallest value.
  • next() moves the cursor forward and returns the value it lands on. It is only called when a next value exists.
  • hasNext() returns true if there is a value after the cursor. It does not move the cursor.

Aim for next and hasNext in O(1) amortized time and O(h) memory, where h is the height of the tree. Copying the whole tree into an array is allowed but uses O(n) memory.

The tree in tests is written in level order with null for missing children. The first operation creates the cursor; the expected output has one entry per operation (null for the constructor).

examples.why: Ascending order is 1, 3, 6, 8, 10, 14. After 3 there are still values left; after 14 there are none.
hasNext only looks ahead. Calling it twice does not skip the 1.

constraints: At most 200 000 calls to next and hasNext
hints: An in-order walk of a search tree visits values in ascending order. The recursive version is easy, but you cannot pause recursion between calls. What could hold its state instead?
Replace the call stack with your own stack. Which nodes are waiting on it at any moment?
Keep a stack of the left spine: push a node and all its left descendants. next() pops the top, then pushes the left spine of that node's right child. hasNext() is just "is the stack non-empty".

explain.intuition:
Recursive in-order traversal visits left subtree, node, right subtree. To make it pausable, keep the recursion's call stack yourself. At any moment the stack holds the nodes whose left side is being explored or done but which have not been returned yet. The smallest unreturned value is always on top.

Start by pushing the root and keep going left, pushing each node. next() pops the top node; that is the answer. Before returning, push the left spine of its right child, because those values come next. Each node is pushed and popped exactly once over the whole walk, so n calls cost O(n) in total: O(1) amortized. The stack never holds more than one path from root to leaf, so memory is O(h). This is how a lazy iterator or a generator over a tree works.
steps: In the constructor, push the root and then follow left pointers, pushing every node.
next(): pop the top node and remember its value.
Push the left spine starting from that node's right child: the child, its left child, and so on.
hasNext(): return whether the stack is non-empty.
pitfalls: Pushing the whole right subtree, or only the right child without its left spine. The next smallest value is the leftmost node of the right subtree.
Doing work in hasNext() that moves the cursor. It must be safe to call any number of times.
Thinking a single next() is O(h) so the bound fails. It can be, but every node is pushed once in total, which makes the average O(1).

solutions.title: Flatten to an array first
solutions.idea: Do a full in-order walk in the constructor and store the values. next and hasNext just move an index.

solutions.title: Stack of the left spine
solutions.idea: Keep only the pending ancestors on a stack. Pop the smallest, then push the left spine of its right child.

followups: Add a prev() that moves the cursor back one step. What extra state do you need?
Write the same cursor as a JavaScript generator function. What plays the role of the stack there?
